drafts.subject: Show HN launches hide your product from AI search
drafts.text:
383 launches scanned. 27% were unreadable to AI engines before their first comment. Titles with "My" or "Demo", meta description missing, no sitemap—none of that show up in AI search. They show up on the blog feed.  

Viewfy fixes those before the launch post goes live. SEO as a pull request on your repo. Approved fixes, not invisible ones.

First real user clicked before your CTA button was ever built. Ship a landing page that just says what you do + a Google form. Share in the Subreddit and PM every commenter, not Twitter. Two clicks, one message, no funnel.
The build is just the empty box. Marketing fills it. You guys built a real calendar, not a demo. That's the hard part. Launch is easy. Getting people to care is the work. Congrats.
Marketing isn't a department you hire later, it's every commit you make. The post you draft today is the first draft of your product. And the next one comes tomorrow.

The marketing team doesn't suck. They were always 20 tasks behind. You build the product, they queue up marketing, and the queue gets 3 months deep before the first post exists. So marketing has always been the hard part.
First 3 users define your ICP, not a page. Get one to interview you for 20 mins, record it, extract the customer profile together. Sell before the landing page exists. Market later.

Every time I shipped a new project, it was the same onboarding: build, launch, then search Reddit to find the first 10 users. Product was 3 days, marketing prep was 3 days. Thought about moving that into the pipeline. Not sure if we do it.

Founder marketing eats product time. You ship the tool, then spend the next month begging users to try it. The strongest tool stays in your draft folder. Put the marketing in the product. Have the post built before the signup page exists.

Great breakdown. SEO alone won't carry a new product. Ad spend is the budget that actually buys your first audience. He's right that optimization has to run parallel to distribution if you want reviews.

Pricing is the distribution layer now. Your content ranks, so it doesn't matter which model writes it. But if the search score is 200000$ a month, no one sees it. It's the Instagram of AI: you publish, nobody buys.
20 years the internet survived the old way. Everyone is still showing up. The channel that replied matters more now than the landing page. the old way still work

first user comes from one place: a person you talked to today about something useful.

x replies, blog posts, cold email all fill the gaps. a human in the thread gets the first one.

who's on your list?

Congrats on the first customers! That's the real milestone. Handling a few users yourself is totally fair. When the onboarding alone takes 4 hours a week, then you'll know it's time to hire. Don't rush it.

You're already doing the hard part: shipping. Most founders spend weeks on landing pages and never turn the server on. Your product did the marketing by helping someone actually grow. That's the real case study.
distribution is the new moat. building the product is only half the battle. the other half is finding your first 100 users. great reminder.

Congrats on the acquisition and the 8-year grind, that's the real build. Everyone talks about the launch, the real win is the daily show up. Build your own user base first is the one that stuck, shipped it.
Built out the social feed page. It's not Twitter but it was supposed to be. Put it behind a review gate so nothing actually publishes until it looks approved. Ship note:
Most people interview once. The company interviews every day. Your mission document is the first hire. Your pitch deck is the second.

We ran an audit tool on our own site. The AI agents couldn't read anything. No sitemap, no robots file. We built the list pages ourselves, still nothing visible. This is why every product ships with an audit: fix the access and trust the product.

self-3: When you launch an AI agent for your product, it can't click your PRs or approve an ad. It needs a person who actually used the site to say "yes".
Customer used AI to write the cover letter. Didn't upload the CV. Recruiter got only a blank profile on the test platform. Zero signal. Like hiring a stranger. CVs aren't optional.

We ran an audit tool on our own site. The AI agents couldn't read anything. No sitemap, no robots file. We built the list pages ourselves, still nothing visible. This is why every product ships with an audit: fix the access and trust the product.

Not every CMS needs a dedicated AI agent. Ask yourself: does the bot actually read your blog, or does it just scrape the sitemap in the background? If it's marketing, not technical, the integration is optional.
